title: Accountant Bali Bookkeeping Onboarding: First 90 Days
contentHtml:
Accountant bali bookkeeping onboarding should begin with an agreed opening period, a complete record map and clear responsibilities. During the first 90 days, the accountant should understand the entity, villas, bank accounts, booking channels, suppliers and owner transactions; identify missing evidence; reconcile selected cash movements; and establish a repeatable monthly close. The aim is not to rush a report, but to make each figure traceable and each unresolved question visible.

Who this applies to

This guide is for Bali villa owners, operators, remote investors, property managers and small companies appointing a bookkeeping provider for the first time or changing from an informal spreadsheet process. It is especially relevant where income arrives through Airbnb, Booking.com, Agoda, direct bookings, management accounts or several bank accounts.

It also applies when a company has older records but no dependable handover. In that situation, the first 90 days are a planning framework for establishing control over the current period while documenting historical gaps. They are not a guaranteed turnaround period. The exact sequence should be adapted to transaction volume, available documents, accounting software, entity structure and the separate responsibilities of any authorised tax adviser.

Bookkeeping is not the same as tax advice, filing, licensing or legal review. A provider may organise evidence and prepare schedules, but tax treatment, submissions and regulatory decisions require the responsible authorised person and a separate engagement where applicable. Bali Accounting’s accounting services should therefore be read alongside the agreed scope, not as a substitute for an engagement letter.

Before the first working session

A productive onboarding starts with a short fact sheet. Record the legal entity name, operating names, villa locations, ownership structure, management arrangement, currency used for reporting and the period that needs attention. Note whether one entity operates several properties, whether the manager holds guest money, and whether the owner pays suppliers personally.

Gather source documents rather than relying only on totals copied into a spreadsheet. Useful evidence includes:

  • Bank statements and cash-count records for each business or property account.
  • OTA reservation exports, payout statements, commission documents and refund records.
  • Direct booking invoices, receipts, deposits and cancellation correspondence.
  • Supplier invoices for utilities, maintenance, cleaning, marketing, repairs and professional fees.
  • Management agreements, owner statements, lease documents and records of reserves.
  • Company registration and accounting-system information relevant to the bookkeeping scope.
  • Schedules showing owner advances, reimbursements, withdrawals and payments made on behalf of the villa.

Do not send passwords in a shared spreadsheet. Use the provider’s approved access process, assign user permissions deliberately and keep a list of accounts granted, changed or withdrawn. Access should be sufficient for the agreed work without giving every person unrestricted control over payments or profile settings.

Agree the reporting questions early. An owner may need property-level income and costs, cash available, unpaid supplier items, owner funding and unresolved payout differences. A manager may need operational spending and upcoming commitments. These are different views of the same records and should not be confused with a promise that bookkeeping alone answers every tax or legal question.

The first 30 days: establish the record map

The first phase is about orientation and evidence. The bookkeeper should document where each important number originates and how it moves through the business. A simple source-to-report map might connect a reservation export to a platform payout, the payout to a bank receipt, and the receipt to the accounting record. For a supplier, it might connect the invoice, approval, payment and bank line.

Separate the following categories from the start:

Illustrative onboarding record map
AreaEvidence to collectQuestion to resolve
BookingsReservation and payout reportsIs the report showing guest charges, deductions or cash received?
BankingStatements and transaction exportsWhich accounts belong to the entity or villa?
SuppliersInvoices, approvals and payment proofWas the cost for one property, several properties or the owner?
Owner activityTransfer notes and funding schedulesWas the movement funding, reimbursement, withdrawal or an operating cost?
ManagementStatements and agreementsWhich deductions are fees, reserves, costs or amounts held for others?

Next, identify the opening point. If prior records are reliable, the opening point may be the last reconciled month. If they are not, label the starting figures as provisional and create an open-item register. Do not present a partial list of balances as a trial balance, and do not invent journal entries merely to make figures appear to agree. Each opening figure should be supported by a statement, schedule, invoice, agreement or clearly documented explanation.

Use the first month to test a manageable selection of evidence. For example, choose one bank account, one OTA payout cycle and a sample of supplier payments. Record what matched, what did not match and why. This is more useful than importing every historical line before the source documents and classifications are understood.

Owners should expect questions about mixed personal and business spending. A payment made from a personal card may still relate to the villa, but its purpose, payee, date and reimbursement status need to be documented. Similarly, a transfer from an owner is not automatically revenue. The bookkeeping record should preserve the distinction between cash movement and income classification for later review.

Days 31 to 60: reconcile and classify

The second phase turns the map into working schedules. Bank reconciliation means comparing recorded transactions with the bank statement and explaining timing differences, duplicates, missing entries, transfers and unidentified items. OTA reconciliation is a separate exercise: reservation value, platform deductions, refunds, reserves and payout timing may appear in different reports.

Keep a missing-document register with an owner, requested date, status and next action. Prioritise evidence that affects cash, ownership, large supplier balances, guest funds, inter-property allocations or adviser questions. A missing small receipt may be tracked without blocking every other task; an unexplained transfer between an owner and company account deserves earlier attention.

Illustrative IDR cash-movement example: suppose a business bank account receives an OTA payout of IDR 18,000,000, pays cleaning suppliers of IDR 3,200,000, pays utilities of IDR 1,050,000 and transfers IDR 4,000,000 to the owner. The selected cash movement schedule is:

Illustrative cash movement schedule, not a trial balance
MovementCash effectRunning cash movement
OTA payout received+IDR 18,000,000IDR 18,000,000
Cleaning payments-IDR 3,200,000IDR 14,800,000
Utility payment-IDR 1,050,000IDR 13,750,000
Owner transfer-IDR 4,000,000IDR 9,750,000

The arithmetic is IDR 18,000,000 minus IDR 3,200,000 minus IDR 1,050,000 minus IDR 4,000,000 equals IDR 9,750,000. That closing movement should be compared with the bank statement for the selected period. The example does not determine revenue, profit, tax, a liability or the correct accounting entry. The OTA report may show gross guest charges and deductions that are not represented by the net receipt, while the owner transfer may require an ownership or funding classification.

Classification should follow evidence and the agreed chart of accounts. Keep property costs distinct where practical, especially when one company operates several villas. Shared costs need an allocation basis recorded in a schedule. Owner payments need a clear description. Refundable guest deposits should not be silently treated as income; see the related guide on refundable deposits and owner statements.

At the end of this phase, the owner should receive an exceptions list, not just a polished number. Exceptions can include an OTA payout with no matching report, a supplier invoice paid from a personal account, an unexplained management deduction or an opening balance lacking evidence. Each item should state what is known, what is missing and who must answer it.

Days 61 to 90: close the process

The third phase tests whether the process can run repeatedly. Agree a monthly collection routine: when bank statements are available, who exports OTA reports, where invoices are uploaded, how managers explain unusual spending and when owners answer questions. The schedule should be adaptable to the villa’s activity rather than treated as a guaranteed completion timetable.

A practical close pack may include a profit-and-loss view, cash movement summary, bank reconciliation status, OTA reconciliation schedule, supplier open items, owner-funding schedule and a list of assumptions. If property-level reporting is needed, show the allocation method and identify costs that remain shared. If cash is held for an owner or guest, show that distinction clearly rather than presenting all bank cash as freely available operating money.

Review the report with questions that test usefulness:

  • Can each material receipt be traced to a platform, direct booking or other source?
  • Can each material payment be traced to an invoice, approval or explanation?
  • Are owner transfers visible separately from operating costs?
  • Do the bank and payout schedules explain timing differences?
  • Are unresolved items assigned to a person and next action?
  • Does the report distinguish bookkeeping facts from tax or legal conclusions?

Where tax records are needed, prepare an evidence pack for the licensed adviser rather than assuming the bookkeeper has made the final determination. The Bali tax consultant evidence-pack guide explains how indexes, reconciliations and questions can be organised without turning bookkeeping into tax advice.

By the end of the planning period, the useful outcome is a controlled routine: source files arrive consistently, bank and platform movements are checked, owner activity is documented, missing evidence is visible and monthly reporting follows an agreed structure. If the first review reveals extensive historical gaps, separate catch-up work may be scoped. The current monthly process should not be delayed indefinitely while every old issue is reconstructed.

What owners get wrong

1. “The bank balance is the profit.” A bank balance includes owner transfers, reserves, deposits, financing, timing differences and payments that may relate to several periods. Correction: ask for a reconciliation and a report that separates operating performance from cash movements.

2. “The OTA payout is the booking revenue.” A payout may be net of commissions, refunds, reserves or other deductions. Correction: retain the reservation report, deduction evidence, payout statement and bank receipt so the adviser can assess the appropriate treatment.

3. “Any owner-funded payment is an expense.” The payment may be an owner advance, reimbursement, capital-related movement or operating cost, depending on the facts. Correction: keep a dated owner-funding schedule with purpose, payee, property, proof and repayment or withdrawal status.

Printable first-90-days checklist

  1. Scope: confirm entity, villas, period, currencies, reporting needs and excluded services.
  2. People: name the owner, manager, bookkeeper and authorised tax adviser responsible for each question.
  3. Access: list bank, OTA, payment, accounting and document-storage access; remove unnecessary permissions.
  4. Sources: collect statements, payout reports, invoices, agreements, owner schedules and management statements.
  5. Opening point: identify the last reliable period or label opening figures provisional.
  6. Missing documents: create a register with priority, owner, status and next action.
  7. Reconciliations: test bank movements, transfers and selected OTA settlements against source evidence.
  8. Classification: separate income evidence, operating costs, owner activity, deposits, reserves and shared costs.
  9. Review: issue an exceptions list and hold an owner review focused on decisions, not unexplained totals.
  10. Monthly routine: agree collection dates, file naming, approval steps, close outputs and escalation of unresolved items.
  11. Adviser handover: index relevant evidence and questions for the responsible authorised person.

Owners who want to compare scope can also review questions to ask before hiring an accountant in Bali and the practical distinction between monthly deliverables and wider advisory work. If the process or required reporting is unclear, a Client Advisory discussion can help define the records and responsibilities before any separate work is agreed. Use the Client Advisory enquiry route rather than assuming consultation, preparation or submission work is included in monthly bookkeeping.

General information only: this article is not tax, legal, accounting or immigration advice and is not evidence of individual professional review. Rules and filing responsibilities can depend on current facts and should be confirmed with the appropriately authorised Indonesian adviser. Preparation or submission work requires a separate engagement and responsible authorised person.

Frequently asked questions

What should I send an accountant before onboarding?

Send entity and property details, bank statements, OTA and direct-booking reports, supplier invoices, management statements, owner-funding records and access information through a secure process. Include a list of known gaps instead of filling them with estimates.

Is 90 days a guaranteed time to finish the books?

No. Ninety days is an adaptable planning framework for establishing the record map, testing reconciliations and agreeing a monthly routine. Missing documents, several properties, historical cleanup and transaction volume may change the sequence and scope.

Can an accountant use my bank balance as the opening figure?

A bank balance can be evidence for a bank account at a specific date, but it does not by itself establish every opening balance or classification. The supporting statement, ownership context, outstanding items and prior records should be reviewed and documented.

How are Airbnb or other OTA payouts handled during onboarding?

The payout should be compared with reservation activity, deductions, refunds, reserves and the bank receipt. The net cash receipt may not answer the separate questions of booking value, operating cost, liability or tax treatment.

Does bookkeeping onboarding include tax filing?

Not automatically. Bookkeeping may organise records and schedules, while tax advice, preparation and submission require the responsible authorised person and a separate engagement. Confirm the boundary in writing before relying on a deliverable.

title: Airbnb Bookkeeping: Cleaning Fees and Extra Guest Charges
primaryKeyword: airbnb bookkeeping cleaning fees guest charges
contentHtml:
Cleaning fees and extra guest charges should be tracked as separate booking components, then reconciled to the Airbnb reservation statement and bank payout. Do not record only the net amount received. A reliable file shows the accommodation charge, cleaning fee, extra guest charge, platform adjustments, fees, refunds and final cash movement for each reservation or settlement period. This helps a Bali villa owner explain revenue, housekeeping costs, outstanding questions and cash without confusing the platform payout with the booking value.

The treatment of a particular charge for Indonesian reporting can depend on the business, contract, taxpayer and transaction facts. This article is a bookkeeping and evidence guide, not tax advice.

Who this applies to

This guide is for Bali villa owners, operators, management companies and bookkeepers who receive Airbnb settlements or use Airbnb reservation records to calculate owner statements. It is especially useful where:

  • Airbnb displays a cleaning fee separately from the nightly accommodation amount.
  • A guest pays an additional amount because the reservation exceeds the included guest count.
  • Housekeeping is paid directly by the villa, manager or owner rather than by Airbnb.
  • The bank receives one combined payout covering several reservations, currencies or adjustments.
  • A management agreement requires revenue and costs to be reported property by property.

It also applies when the villa uses several channels. Airbnb may use different descriptions, settlement dates or fee structures from Booking.com, direct bookings or a channel manager. A consistent internal schedule can still assign each booking to the correct villa and charge type.

What each charge means in the records

A cleaning fee charged to a guest is a booking-side amount. It is not automatically the same thing as the housekeeping expense paid to a cleaner. The guest charge answers, “What did the reservation include?” The supplier invoice or payment answers, “What did the villa spend?” These two records may have different dates, descriptions and amounts.

An extra guest charge is also a booking-side amount. Keep it separate from the base accommodation charge when the platform or reservation record identifies it separately. A clear schedule lets the owner see whether the amount relates to an additional person, an amended reservation, an extra service or another guest-requested item. If the description is unclear, flag it for management or tax-adviser review rather than guessing.

Useful booking evidence normally includes the reservation ID, property, guest dates, booking date, currency, accommodation amount, cleaning fee, extra guest charge, discounts, refunds, platform fees, payout date and bank reference. Preserve the original platform export or statement, not only a manually edited spreadsheet.

Suggested Airbnb booking evidence schedule
ColumnWhy it mattersExample source
Reservation ID and villaConnects the booking to the correct property and guest stayAirbnb reservation export
Accommodation amountSeparates nightly or stay revenue from other chargesReservation detail
Cleaning feeIdentifies the guest-facing charge without assuming the costGuest receipt or payout report
Extra guest chargeExplains an amount caused by occupancy or a reservation amendmentReservation amendment
Platform fee or adjustmentBridges booking components to the settlement amountAirbnb earnings statement
Supplier evidenceSupports the separate housekeeping cost recordInvoice, receipt or payment approval
Payout date and bank referenceConnects the platform settlement to actual cashBank statement

Where a manager collects the payout, also retain the manager statement showing the amount received, deductions, transfers to the owner and any reserve retained. A bank deposit alone cannot explain which bookings created the cash.

A practical reconciliation workflow

Start with the reservation-level evidence, then work toward the settlement and bank account. This avoids treating a bank credit as the complete source record.

  1. Collect the period export. Download the Airbnb earnings, reservation and adjustment reports for the period being reviewed. Record the report date and account or listing covered.
  2. Identify the booking components. For each reservation, list accommodation, cleaning fee, extra guest charge, discounts, refunds and other separately displayed items. Use one row per reservation or a documented settlement-level schedule where the platform report is settlement based.
  3. Separate platform deductions. Show service fees, corrections, currency movements and other deductions in their own columns. Do not hide them by entering only the net payout as revenue.
  4. Match the settlement. Add the relevant booking components, subtract documented deductions and compare the result to the platform settlement. A difference should become an open item, not a forced adjustment.
  5. Match the bank. Compare the settlement date, currency, amount and bank reference to the bank statement. If one deposit contains several settlements, keep a deposit-composition schedule.
  6. Attach operating costs separately. Match cleaning and linen invoices or approved payments to the stays or period they support. Do not net the cost against the guest cleaning fee in the booking schedule.
  7. Review exceptions. Investigate cancelled stays, partial refunds, amended guest counts, missing supplier documents, duplicate imports and deposits that remain unmatched.

The accounting period used for the books may not be identical to the stay date, payout date or supplier invoice date. The responsible bookkeeper should apply the agreed bookkeeping basis consistently and document timing differences. Where the correct treatment affects tax or statutory reporting, refer the question to the authorised adviser.

Illustrative IDR worked example

The following is an illustrative cash-movement and evidence schedule only. It is not a tax calculation and does not prescribe the treatment of any charge.

Illustrative reservation and settlement in IDR
ItemAmount
Accommodation chargeIDR 4,800,000
Guest cleaning feeIDR 600,000
Extra guest chargeIDR 400,000
Guest-facing booking totalIDR 5,800,000
Platform fee shown on statementIDR 870,000
Expected platform payoutIDR 4,930,000
Housekeeping payment recorded separatelyIDR 600,000

The arithmetic is: IDR 4,800,000 + IDR 600,000 + IDR 400,000 = IDR 5,800,000. Then IDR 5,800,000 − IDR 870,000 = IDR 4,930,000. If the bank receives IDR 4,930,000, the platform-to-bank bridge agrees for this illustrative reservation. The separate housekeeping payment does not reduce the platform payout; it is an operating cash movement supported by its own invoice or approval.

If the bank instead receives IDR 4,730,000, the difference is IDR 200,000. That difference could reflect a further platform adjustment, currency conversion, reserve, refund or an error. The correct response is to locate the supporting statement and record an open question. It is not to reduce the cleaning fee or invent an unexplained journal entry merely to make the numbers agree.

What owners get wrong

  1. Correction one: recording only the net payout. A bank import of IDR 4,930,000 may be convenient, but it hides the IDR 5,800,000 booking components and IDR 870,000 platform fee. Keep a gross-to-net bridge so the owner can trace the settlement.
  2. Correction two: treating the cleaning fee as the cleaner’s pay. A guest may be charged IDR 600,000 while the approved cleaner invoice is a different amount, covers several villas or is paid on another date. Record the guest charge and supplier cost as separate evidence streams.
  3. Correction three: burying extra guest charges in accommodation revenue. Combining every guest-facing amount may make the report shorter, but it removes useful operational information. Preserve the platform label and explain any internal grouping in the chart of accounts or reporting notes.

Owners also commonly compare a monthly bank total with a monthly reservation total without checking settlement timing. A stay near month-end may be paid in the following period, while a payout can include reservations from different stay dates. A short timing schedule prevents a normal cut-off difference from being mistaken for missing revenue.

Reporting, controls and owner review

A useful monthly owner pack should show more than Airbnb revenue. Include a channel summary, property allocation, cleaning and linen costs, platform deductions, refunds, owner transfers, reserves and unresolved exceptions. The report should distinguish operating performance from cash availability. A high booking total does not mean the same amount is available for withdrawal.

For several villas, require a property code on every reservation, supplier document and bank allocation. Shared housekeeping purchases should be assigned using a documented basis, such as a specific stay, villa or approved period. Do not silently split a receipt across properties because the amounts appear convenient. Keep the allocation note with the source document.

Access controls matter as well. Limit who can change the Airbnb payout account, reservation exports or bookkeeping categories. Keep a record of manual corrections, especially where a reservation was amended after checkout. A second-person review can focus on large adjustments, refunds, unusual extra guest charges and unmatched deposits.

Owners who need specialist support can review Airbnb bookkeeping for Bali villas. Related reading includes reconciling Airbnb and Booking.com payouts, Airbnb refunds, cancellations and payout reserves and refundable deposits and owner statements.

Printable monthly checklist

Use this list as a practical collection and review control. Adapt the period and responsible person to the villa’s operating arrangements.

  1. Download Airbnb reservation, earnings and adjustment exports.
  2. Confirm the report period, listing names, currency and export date.
  3. List accommodation, cleaning fees and extra guest charges separately.
  4. Record discounts, refunds, cancellations and amended reservations.
  5. List platform fees and other deductions from the settlement statement.
  6. Build a gross-to-net bridge for each settlement or documented batch.
  7. Match each settlement to the bank statement and bank reference.
  8. List housekeeping, linen and turnover costs from invoices or approved receipts.
  9. Check that supplier costs are not netted against guest charges.
  10. Assign each booking and cost to the correct villa or shared-cost schedule.
  11. Review unusual guest charges, duplicate rows and unexplained differences.
  12. Prepare an open-items register for missing evidence or adviser questions.
  13. Archive exports, statements, invoices and reconciliation notes together.
  14. Ask the authorised tax adviser about any classification or reporting question before submission work.

This checklist is general information only and is not tax, legal, accounting-opinion or immigration advice. It does not state a tax rate, filing deadline, threshold or required treatment. Preparation or submission work requires the responsible authorised person and a separate engagement; it is not automatically included in monthly bookkeeping. For a scoped discussion, owners can use the Client Advisory enquiry route.

Frequently asked questions

Should the Airbnb cleaning fee be recorded as revenue?

Keep it identifiable as a guest-facing booking component and reconcile it to the platform statement. Whether it is grouped or classified in a particular reporting or tax account depends on the entity and facts, so confirm that treatment with the responsible authorised adviser.

Is an extra guest charge the same as accommodation income?

Not necessarily for internal bookkeeping. Preserve the platform’s description and show the charge separately before any approved reporting grouping. This keeps the reservation evidence clear and helps explain amended guest counts.

Can I record only the amount Airbnb deposits into the bank?

You can use the deposit as the cash evidence, but it should not be the only booking record. Retain a gross-to-net bridge showing reservation components, platform deductions, refunds and the final payout.

How should cleaning costs be connected to guest cleaning fees?

Maintain two linked schedules: one for guest charges and one for supplier costs. Match invoices or approved payments to stays, villas or periods where possible, but do not assume the amounts must be equal.

What if one Airbnb payout covers several villas?

Prepare a deposit-composition schedule that allocates each settlement to the relevant reservation and villa. Investigate any residual difference using the platform statement, bank reference and adjustment records rather than forcing an allocation.

title: Rental Property Accounting: Records for Repairs and Improvements
primaryKeyword: rental property accounting repairs improvements records
contentHtml:
For rental property accounting repairs improvements records, start by recording what work was done, why it was needed, which part of the property it affected, and how it was paid. Routine work that restores an existing item may differ from a project that changes or adds to the property. Do not decide from the invoice label or amount alone: keep the evidence together and ask your accountant or qualified tax adviser about the appropriate treatment.

Who this applies to

This guide is for Bali villa owners, operators and property managers who need their books to explain maintenance spending. It is especially useful when a property has frequent small jobs alongside occasional renovation work, when a manager pays suppliers on an owner’s behalf, or when different villas share contractors and materials.

The core task is record-keeping, not making a legal or tax determination. A bookkeeper can organise invoices, trace cash movements, identify missing information and flag ambiguous items. The appropriate accountant applies the accounting basis and policy for the reporting entity. A licensed tax adviser considers tax treatment in light of the taxpayer, transaction and relevant rules. Those decisions may need more than a description such as maintenance, renovation or upgrade.

Owners should also distinguish the person responsible for the property from the entity that paid the bill. A villa may be owned, leased, managed or operated through different arrangements. Record who ordered the work, who received the service, whose account paid, and whether anyone is due reimbursement. If several properties are involved, identify the relevant villa and record any allocation basis for shared work rather than silently assigning the full cost to one property.

How to think about repairs and larger work

A useful first question is whether the work mainly restores an existing item to its prior working condition, or creates a meaningful addition or change. For example, repairing a leaking pipe or replacing a broken lock may be routine maintenance. A project that adds a new room, installs a substantially different system, or changes the property’s function may warrant closer review as a possible improvement. These are prompts to gather evidence, not automatic accounting or tax classifications.

Real projects can include both kinds of work. A contractor might repair damaged wiring while also installing a new electrical system. A single invoice could bundle labour, materials, transport and several rooms. In that situation, request a clear scope or itemisation from the supplier if available. Record what can be supported, and mark unclear portions for review. Do not make up a split merely to force a clean-looking expense category.

Consider the nature of the work, the item affected, the property’s condition before and after, the project’s purpose, and the applicable reporting policy. Cost, expected useful life and materiality may be relevant to the accountant’s decision, but none is a stand-alone rule for owners to apply. Nor does the word renovation on a quote prove that the full amount is an improvement. Equally, calling a project maintenance does not settle its accounting or tax treatment.

Keep the bookkeeping record factual: date, supplier, property, work description, amount, payment reference and supporting document. A separate review note can state that the classification is unresolved, who should decide it, and what evidence remains outstanding. This is more reliable than hiding uncertainty in a broad repairs account.

Build an evidence trail for each job

A useful file lets a reviewer connect the business purpose to the work, invoice and payment. Collect records as the work is approved and completed, not only when month-end reporting or an adviser request makes the gap obvious. Save original supplier documents and relevant messages in a consistent location. A brief index can link the documents without replacing them.

Evidence to keep with a villa maintenance or improvement item
RecordWhat it helps establishUseful detail to capture
Request or approvalWhy work was commissioned and who authorised itVilla, problem or project purpose, approval date
Quote and work scopeWhat the supplier expected to doRoom or asset, proposed work, inclusions and exclusions
Invoice or receiptSupplier, billed work and amountInvoice date, supplier identity, itemisation, currency
Completion evidenceWhat was actually completedCompletion message, handover note, photos or changed scope
Payment supportHow the cash left the accountBank reference, transfer date, payer and payee
Review noteQuestions requiring accounting or tax judgmentUnclear scope, mixed work, adviser question and status

Photographs can help show the condition before and after, but do not replace a supplier invoice or explain the financial movement. Keep a concise note identifying the villa, area, date and what each photo shows. If a manager pays from a float, retain the manager’s expense statement and the underlying supplier evidence, then document how any reimbursement was settled.

For work paid across instalments, retain the quote, each invoice or payment request, and evidence of each transfer. Do not treat a deposit as proof that all work was completed. If the final bill differs from the quote, ask for the reason and revised scope. A missing invoice should be logged openly, with the evidence requested and follow-up owner, rather than silently replaced by a bank description.

Illustrative IDR example: trace the cash, not the classification

The following example is illustrative only. It demonstrates a selected cash-movement schedule; it is not a complete account balance, trial balance, tax calculation or conclusion about treatment. Assume an operator pays IDR 7,000,000 for a documented pipe repair and IDR 45,000,000 for a separately scoped project that changes the villa’s outdoor area. The bank statement shows both payments to suppliers.

Illustrative selected payment evidence schedule
Work referenceSupplier paymentEvidence to match
Pipe repairIDR 7,000,000Repair invoice, villa reference and bank transfer
Outdoor-area projectIDR 45,000,000Scope, invoice, completion note and bank transfer
Total of these two cash paymentsIDR 52,000,000IDR 7,000,000 + IDR 45,000,000 = IDR 52,000,000

The arithmetic explains only the two payments in this example. It does not establish whether either amount should be expensed, recorded as an asset, allocated over time, or treated in a particular way for tax. The outdoor project’s description suggests a question for the accountant, not a predetermined answer. The owner should preserve its scope and completion evidence and ask the adviser to decide treatment under the relevant reporting framework and facts.

If the project invoice combines the repair and outdoor work without detail, ask the contractor for an accurate breakdown where possible. If no reliable breakdown is available, preserve the invoice as received, document the limitation and seek advice. Do not invent an allocation or balancing journal entry to make the schedule look complete.

Month-end workflow and useful reporting

A dependable monthly process ties work orders to supplier records and then to the bank or payment record. First, gather invoices and approvals. Next, check that each item identifies the correct supplier, property and work. Match payments to bank activity, noting deposits, instalments, reimbursements or payment by a manager. Then flag incomplete, duplicated or mixed-scope documents.

For management reporting, retain the distinction between cash paid and the classification used in the accounts. A large project can create a substantial cash outflow even if the accountant’s reporting treatment spreads its effect over time. Conversely, the fact that a payment was made does not prove a complete invoice or that the expense belongs to the entity whose bank account paid it. A clear report can show property spending and open questions without presenting unresolved judgments as settled.

Where the property manager collects the records, agree who will obtain missing documents and when they will be handed over as part of the close process. Separate villa folders, consistent file names and a simple open-item register make follow-up easier. If an owner pays a supplier personally, record the payment evidence and identify the intended reimbursement or funding explanation for review; do not automatically classify it as a property expense without checking who received the work and the arrangement.

For context on other record-keeping issues, see our guides to refundable deposits and owner statements, a practical Bali villa chart of accounts, and preparing an evidence pack for a Bali tax consultant. Villa financial reporting support is described on our villa financial reporting service page.

What owners get wrong

  1. Correction: the invoice label is not the conclusion. A supplier’s use of maintenance, renovation or upgrade helps describe the job, but does not settle how the entity should report it. Keep the scope and ask the accountant to assess the facts and applicable policy.
  2. Correction: price alone does not decide. A high bill is not automatically an improvement, and a low bill is not automatically a repair. Document the work, affected item and purpose; leave materiality and classification judgments to the responsible professional.
  3. Correction: a bank line is not enough evidence. A transfer proves a cash movement, not the full business purpose or scope. Match it to an invoice, approval and completion evidence, and record who paid if it was not the entity account.

Printable maintenance and project record checklist

Use this list for each job or project. Tick what is present, assign a person to collect what is missing, and keep unresolved classification questions visible for the adviser.

  • Identify the job: record the property, room or asset, supplier, request date and concise description.
  • Preserve the approval: save the request, approval and any agreed change in scope.
  • Describe the work: retain the quote, work order and itemised scope where available; distinguish separate jobs on a bundled document if supplier support exists.
  • Verify completion: save an invoice, completion confirmation and relevant handover evidence; note work that remains unfinished.
  • Match the cash: record the amount, payment date, payer, payee, bank reference and any instalment or reimbursement link.
  • Check property assignment: note which villa benefited and document the basis for any shared-cost allocation.
  • Log exceptions: list missing, unclear, changed or duplicate documents and assign follow-up responsibility.
  • Ask for review: mark mixed repair and project scope, material changes or uncertain classifications for the accountant or qualified tax adviser.
  • File consistently: use a stable folder and filename that connects the invoice to the property and payment record.
  • Close the loop: carry outstanding questions into the next close until evidence is collected or the adviser’s decision is documented.

Owners looking for support organising these schedules can discuss the bookkeeping and reporting scope through Bali Accounting’s Client Advisory team. Any accounting classification or tax work must be agreed within the appropriate separate engagement and handled by the responsible authorised person; it is not assumed to be part of monthly bookkeeping.

Property structure, reporting framework, contracts and facts can change the appropriate treatment. Consult your accountant and a qualified Indonesian tax adviser for advice relevant to your circumstances.

Frequently asked questions

Is a villa repair always an operating expense?

No. The word repair is not enough to determine treatment. Record what was restored, the item affected and the supporting documents, then ask the accountant to apply the relevant reporting policy and facts.

Does a large invoice automatically count as an improvement?

No. Amount alone does not decide classification. The scope, purpose, asset affected and applicable accounting policy may matter. Keep an itemised scope and refer the decision to the responsible accountant.

What if one invoice includes repairs and upgrade work?

Request an accurate breakdown from the supplier if available. Keep the original invoice and supporting scope, note any uncertainty, and ask the accountant how to handle the mixed work. Do not create an unsupported split.

What evidence should I keep if a villa manager pays?

Keep the supplier invoice, manager’s expense statement, approval and evidence of the payment. Record which property benefited and how the manager’s payment was settled or remains due.

Can my bookkeeper decide the tax treatment?

Bookkeeping can organise evidence and flag questions, but it does not automatically include a tax determination or submission. Ask a qualified tax adviser to assess the facts, and confirm the engagement and authorised responsibility separately.

title: Multi-Currency Bookkeeping for Bali Villas: Understanding Exchange Differences
contentHtml:
Multi-currency bookkeeping for Bali villas means preserving each transaction’s original currency, documenting how it was converted, and recording the resulting cash movement in the company’s reporting records. Exchange differences can arise when conversion rates differ between the transaction, settlement and later measurement of an unpaid balance. Keep the evidence trail visible; ask a qualified adviser to confirm the accounting and tax treatment applicable to the entity.

Who this applies to

This guide is for villa owners and operators whose records contain more than one currency. A PT PMA may receive an online travel agency (OTA) payout in a foreign currency, pay an overseas supplier, hold funds in a foreign-currency account, or receive owner funding from abroad. Even where guest prices are quoted in a foreign currency, the payout may be converted before it reaches the company’s bank. The booking currency, settlement currency and bank-account currency are not necessarily the same.

The issue is not limited to large international transfers. It can arise in a monthly platform reconciliation, a card charge for software, a refundable guest balance, an owner advance, or an invoice that remains unpaid at month end. A reliable record should let a reviewer move from the source document to the amount recorded, and then to the bank or payment evidence.

It is also useful for an owner comparing reports prepared in different currencies. A statement in a home currency can help with management decisions, but it should not obscure the source currency or replace the company’s records. Agree with the responsible accountant which currency the bookkeeping reports use and how any owner-facing conversion is presented.

Separate the currencies and the questions

Start by labeling the currencies involved rather than treating “foreign currency” as one field. For each transaction, identify the currency on the invoice or reservation, the currency actually paid or received, the account where funds settled, and the currency used in the bookkeeping records. Preserve the original amount and the conversion evidence as separate facts.

Next, distinguish a currency conversion from an exchange difference. A conversion occurs when a payment provider or bank exchanges one currency for another. An exchange difference is the change in the reporting-currency value of a foreign-currency amount between relevant measurement points. For example, an unpaid supplier invoice may have one recorded value when first recognized and a different value when paid. The cash movement is real; the difference is not an extra bank transfer.

Another distinction is between a transaction already settled and an amount still outstanding. A paid invoice can be compared with its settlement evidence. An unpaid invoice or foreign-currency balance may require a separate period-end assessment under the accounting approach applicable to the company. Do not assume that the same rate, treatment, or timing applies to every balance.

These are bookkeeping distinctions, not a determination of the correct accounting framework or tax result for a particular PT PMA. Provide the entity’s governing documents, prior reporting approach and transaction records to the appropriately qualified adviser when those decisions need confirmation.

Build a traceable record workflow

  1. Keep the source record. Save the reservation detail, OTA statement, supplier invoice, owner-funding document or other evidence showing the original currency and amount. Retain the date, counterparty and business purpose where available.
  2. Capture settlement evidence. Save the payout or payment-provider statement and the bank statement. Record the currency sent or received, the currency credited or debited, the rate or conversion amount shown by the provider, and any separately stated fees.
  3. Match the movement. Connect the booking or invoice to its payout or payment and then to the bank line. Note timing differences, grouped settlements, refunds and deductions rather than forcing unlike amounts to match.
  4. Keep rate evidence with the period. If the bookkeeping process uses an agreed rate source for transactions not settled directly by a provider, document the source, date and method. Ask the responsible accountant or adviser to approve the method and explain how exceptions are handled. Do not select a rate simply because it creates a preferred result.
  5. List outstanding foreign-currency items. At close, identify unpaid bills, receivables and account balances in their original currency. Include the source amount, recorded value, settlement status and supporting references in a review schedule.
  6. Explain differences. Label each difference as an item to investigate, such as a provider conversion, separately stated bank fee, refund, timing item or potential exchange movement. Do not use a general “FX” line to hide an unexplained bank variance.

For platform activity, reconcile the reservation-level amounts to the platform statement, deductions and bank receipt. A payout can combine several stays and include commissions or adjustments. The dedicated OTA payout reconciliation workflow explains how to connect those records without mistaking a net deposit for the full booking activity.

Where foreign currency relates to owner funding, document who transferred funds, which entity received them, the amount and currency, and the stated purpose. Keep that evidence distinct from rental revenue and operating receipts. See the PT PMA owner funding records guide for a related documentation workflow.

Illustrative IDR worked example

The schedule below is a deliberately simple illustration, not a trial balance, accounting policy, tax calculation or advice on a current exchange rate. Assume a supplier invoice is for USD 1,000. For illustration only, the company’s records first show an equivalent of IDR 15,000,000 using an assumed rate of IDR 15,000 per USD. When paid, the bank evidence shows that USD 1,000 cost IDR 15,200,000. No separate bank fee is assumed.

Illustrative evidence schedule for one supplier payment
Evidence or movementOriginal amountIllustrative IDR amountWhat it supports
Supplier invoice and initial recordUSD 1,000IDR 15,000,000Initial documented value, using the assumed example rate
Bank settlement for paymentUSD 1,000IDR 15,200,000Cash paid, based on the illustrative bank evidence
Difference between the two valuesSame USD 1,000 obligationIDR 200,000Amount for review under the company’s accounting approach

Arithmetic: IDR 15,200,000 paid minus IDR 15,000,000 initially recorded equals IDR 200,000. The USD obligation shown on the invoice and settlement remains USD 1,000. The IDR cash movement is IDR 15,200,000. The IDR 200,000 is a difference between two recorded values, not an additional payment.

Keep the invoice, bank statement and any conversion confirmation together so a reviewer can verify the schedule. Whether and where the difference is presented depends on the applicable accounting policy and facts. If the bank charged a separate fee, show it as its own evidenced movement rather than folding it into this example’s difference. This schedule deliberately shows selected evidence only; it is not a complete ledger or trial balance.

Month-end review and useful reporting

A useful close links foreign-currency items to a source document, settlement status and a clear explanation. For bank accounts held in a foreign currency, compare the statement’s currency balance with the bookkeeping record and investigate unmatched transactions. For unpaid invoices and receivables, preserve the original currency amount and flag items requiring a period-end valuation decision. Keep the selected exchange-rate evidence and the method used accessible to the person responsible for the close.

Management reporting should distinguish operational performance from currency movement. A villa can have steady booking activity while the IDR equivalent of foreign-currency receipts changes. Conversely, the bank balance may rise because a payout arrived near month end even though the related booking activity belongs to a different period. Explain material movements in plain language, with links to the underlying schedule rather than relying on a single unexplained “FX gain or loss” label.

When owner reporting uses another currency, state whether figures are translated for presentation and how that translation was prepared. Do not combine company cash, owner funds and a converted owner summary into one figure without a reconciliation. The villa owner management pack guide discusses how to connect reported results with cash movement and open items.

What owners get wrong

  • Correction 1: A bank deposit is not always the booking amount. A platform may deduct commissions, refunds or other adjustments, or convert the payout. Reconcile the reservation and platform evidence to the net deposit; don’t record the bank receipt as a substitute for the supporting booking detail.
  • Correction 2: A changed IDR value is not automatically a cash gain or loss. A difference may relate to an unpaid balance, conversion or fee. Identify what happened and when, and ask the responsible accountant to confirm its classification. Do not invent a journal entry to make a schedule appear to balance.
  • Correction 3: One convenient rate is not a universal answer. The relevant treatment may depend on the transaction, the entity’s reporting basis and its accounting policy. Keep rate sources and dates, document the method, and refer policy or tax questions to a qualified adviser.

Also avoid deleting the original-currency figure after converting it to IDR. Without that amount, a reviewer may be unable to compare the invoice, payout statement and bank movement or explain a later settlement difference.

Printable multi-currency close checklist

Use this list as a practical record-collection aid. Adapt it to the entity, systems and agreed bookkeeping scope; it does not replace review by the responsible professional.

  • Entity and account: Confirm the entity, property or activity, bank account and account currency in the schedule.
  • Source: File each invoice, booking report, owner-funding document, refund notice or other evidence with its original currency and amount.
  • Settlement: Attach the platform, card-provider or bank statement and identify the currency actually received or paid.
  • Conversion: Record the provider’s conversion details or the documented rate source and date used for the record.
  • Fees and deductions: Identify separately stated charges, commissions, refunds and reserves; match each to evidence.
  • Matching: Link transaction references to bank lines and list timing differences or grouped payouts that remain open.
  • Open items: List foreign-currency invoices, receivables and account balances still outstanding at close, retaining the source-currency amount.
  • Difference review: Explain each unresolved difference and mark questions for the responsible accountant or licensed tax adviser.
  • Reporting: State the reporting currency and label any owner-facing translation, keeping it separate from the original evidence.
  • Approval and filing: Keep the schedule, supporting documents, review notes and any approved corrections together in the company’s record system.

For an agreed bookkeeping scope, Bali Accounting’s PT PMA villa bookkeeping service can help organize transaction evidence and recurring reconciliations. Scope, close arrangements and any onboarding period are planning matters to agree with the firm; timing depends on the records available and is not guaranteed. Bookkeeping does not automatically include tax advice, preparation or submission. Those services require a separate engagement and work by the responsible authorised person.

For a conversation about fit and scope, contact the firm through Client Advisory.

General information only: This article explains record-keeping concepts and is not tax, legal, accounting-policy or investment advice for an individual business. It is not evidence of professional review. Ask a qualified Indonesian tax adviser or other appropriately licensed professional to assess your company’s circumstances, accounting treatment and filing obligations.

Frequently asked questions

What is an exchange difference in villa bookkeeping?

It is a change in the reporting-currency value of a foreign-currency amount between relevant measurement points. Keep the original amount and evidence; the responsible accountant should confirm how the difference is treated.

Should I record the booking currency or the payout currency?

Preserve both where they differ. The booking or invoice evidence shows the source amount, while the payout and bank records show how settlement occurred. Reconcile the complete path.

Which exchange rate should a Bali villa use?

There is no single rate recommendation for every transaction or entity in this guide. Document the source, date and method used, and have the responsible accountant or qualified adviser confirm the appropriate approach.

Is a foreign-currency bank balance the same as an exchange gain or loss?

No. The balance is a cash amount in its account currency. Its reporting-currency value may change, but the accounting treatment depends on the applicable reporting approach and should be reviewed.

Does monthly bookkeeping include tax filing or tax advice?

Not automatically. Bookkeeping scope should be agreed separately from tax advice, preparation or submission, which requires a separate engagement and the responsible authorised person.

title: Bank Reconciliation for Bali Villas: How to Resolve Unmatched Transactions
primaryKeyword: bank reconciliation bali villa unmatched transactions
contentHtml:
Bank reconciliation for a Bali villa means comparing each account’s bank statement with the records kept for that account, then investigating differences instead of forcing a match. For an unmatched transaction, first check the date, amount, reference and supporting evidence. Record what is known, identify what is still unclear, and leave the item visibly open until it can be explained.

A careful reconciliation does more than confirm that two balances agree. It helps an owner see which cash movements are supported, which transactions may have been recorded twice or missed, and which questions need an answer from a manager, bookkeeper or qualified adviser.

What a bank reconciliation shows

A bank statement is the bank’s record of activity in an account. The bookkeeping records are the business’s record of cash movements in that account. Reconciliation compares the two over the same period and account. Each statement line should be matched to an entry in the books, or listed as an open difference with a reason and next step.

The goal is not to make every line match by changing figures until the totals agree. A difference may be a normal timing issue, such as a transfer recorded in the books near month-end that appears on the statement later. It may instead point to a missing record, duplicate entry, wrong amount, bank fee, refund, foreign-currency conversion or transaction whose purpose has not yet been confirmed.

Keep each bank account separate, including operating accounts, reserve accounts and payment-provider accounts where relevant. Reconcile the same period shown on the statement and retain the statement itself. If the statement is in a different currency from the bookkeeping records, keep the original currency, the recorded conversion information and any applicable exchange-rate evidence together; do not treat a difference as explained merely because currencies are involved.

For villa operations, several evidence streams may meet at the bank: online travel agency payouts, direct guest payments, supplier transfers, card settlements, owner funding and transfers between accounts. The bank line confirms that cash moved. It does not always establish the underlying booking, supplier, purpose or appropriate accounting classification. For payout matching, see the Bali villa OTA payout reconciliation workflow.

Who this applies to

This process is useful for owners and operators who receive villa income or pay operating costs through a company or property bank account. It is also relevant to managers preparing owner statements, remote owners checking monthly reporting, and teams bringing older or incomplete records up to date.

It matters especially where the account handles several kinds of cash movement: platform settlements, direct reservations, guest refunds, supplier bills, maintenance spending and owner transfers. A payment from an owner and a guest receipt may both increase the bank balance, but they do not mean the same thing. Likewise, cash paid out to an owner should not automatically be treated as a villa operating cost. Classification depends on the facts and the entity’s records.

If a manager holds guest funds or refundable deposits, reconcile the bank movement against the management statement and the supporting guest or owner detail. Bank reconciliation alone cannot show whether a deposit remains repayable or whether a deduction is supported. For that distinction, read the guide to refundable deposits and owner statements.

A practical workflow for unmatched items

Work through the account in a repeatable order. Start with a complete statement and a defined period; a cropped screenshot or list of selected transactions may omit the opening balance, bank charges or later reversals. Confirm the account name, currency and statement dates. Then compare statement lines with the bookkeeping detail using amount, date, payee or payer, reference and context.

  1. Match clear items. Connect each statement transaction to the corresponding recorded cash movement. Keep a reference to the invoice, payout report, receipt, approval or transfer evidence where available.
  2. Check timing. If an item appears in one record but not the other, look at the transaction date, settlement date and statement period. A payment initiated before the period ends may clear later; document it as a timing difference only when evidence supports that explanation.
  3. Investigate the details. Search the relevant platform export, bank advice, supplier invoice, payment confirmation, manager statement and internal approvals. Compare the gross booking information with the net cash received where fees, refunds or adjustments may be involved.
  4. Log what remains open. Note the amount, date, account, reference, evidence already reviewed, question still unanswered, person responsible and follow-up action. Set a review date based on the business’s close process, not an assumed universal deadline.
  5. Resolve only when supported. Once evidence explains the difference, update the bookkeeping through the normal review process and preserve a note linking the change to its support. If the reason or classification remains uncertain, escalate it rather than guessing.

For older periods, reconstructing a reconciliation may require statements, platform exports and records from a previous bookkeeper. Keep missing evidence visible rather than marking an item resolved because it is old. A missing-document register for catch-up bookkeeping can help distinguish records requested from differences actually explained.

Common unmatched transactions and what to check

Use the table as an investigation prompt, not as a rule that determines accounting treatment. One bank movement can have several possible explanations, so follow the supporting records and ask for clarification where needed.

Unmatched transaction investigation guide
What you seeEvidence to checkRecord the open question
Platform deposit differs from booking totalsPayout report, reservation detail, fee statement, refund or adjustment recordWhich reservations and deductions make up this settlement?
Supplier payment has no clear invoice matchInvoice, payment approval, supplier name and transfer referenceWhich service or property does the payment relate to?
Bank fee appears without a book entryStatement detail and bank fee schedule or adviceIs this an account charge, payment fee or another type of deduction?
Owner transfer has no stated purposeTransfer confirmation, owner communication and entity recordsIs this funding, reimbursement, repayment or another movement?
Refund or reversal appears after the original itemOriginal transaction, refund confirmation and guest or supplier correspondenceWhich earlier receipt or payment is being reversed or adjusted?
Same amount appears twiceTransaction references, dates, bank lines and source documentsAre these separate movements, a duplicate record or a reversal and re-posting?

Illustrative IDR cash movement schedule

The following is an illustrative cash movement schedule for one bank account, not a trial balance or a tax calculation. It shows how a statement balance can be traced using explicit movements. The business still needs supporting evidence to explain the purpose and bookkeeping classification of each item.

Illustrative statement movement for one period
MovementAmount (IDR)Running balance (IDR)
Opening statement balance12,000,00012,000,000
OTA payout received+8,400,00020,400,000
Owner transfer received+2,000,00022,400,000
Supplier payment-5,250,00017,150,000
Bank charge-25,00017,125,000
Transfer out to owner-1,000,00016,125,000

Arithmetic check: IDR 12,000,000 + IDR 8,400,000 + IDR 2,000,000 - IDR 5,250,000 - IDR 25,000 - IDR 1,000,000 = IDR 16,125,000. If the closing statement balance is IDR 16,125,000, these selected movements explain the statement’s cash bridge. They do not, by themselves, prove that the payout, owner transfers or supplier payment have been recorded or classified correctly in the books. Keep the relevant payout report, transfer details and invoice with the reconciliation.

What owners get wrong

  • Correction 1: Treating a matching balance as proof every transaction is right. Two records can end at the same balance while individual movements are missing, duplicated or misclassified. Match statement lines, review open items and retain source evidence; do not rely on the closing number alone.
  • Correction 2: Calling every difference a timing issue. Timing is a supported explanation only when the transaction can be traced and its later settlement or clearance is checked. An unexplained amount should stay open, with its evidence gap and follow-up recorded.
  • Correction 3: Using a suspense or owner account to make the difference disappear. A temporary label does not explain a movement. Record the uncertainty and ask the responsible person for documents or context. Confirm classification through the appropriate bookkeeping review and, where needed, a qualified adviser.

Another common source of confusion is comparing different periods or accounts. A platform payout may land in one account and then be transferred to another; counting both receipts as villa income would confuse cash movement with the underlying activity. Show the receiving and sending account records together and document the transfer trail.

Printable reconciliation checklist

Use this checklist for a monthly close or adapt it to the business’s agreed reporting cycle. A marked box should mean the work was completed or the exception is clearly logged—not simply that someone looked at the report.

  • [ ] Gather the complete bank statement for each account and confirm account, currency and period.
  • [ ] Obtain the bookkeeping transaction detail for the same account and period.
  • [ ] Confirm the opening and closing statement balances against the source statement.
  • [ ] Match each bank line to recorded activity using amount, date, reference and context.
  • [ ] Compare OTA and payment-provider receipts with payout statements, fees, refunds and adjustments.
  • [ ] Match supplier payments to invoices, approvals and the relevant villa or cost context.
  • [ ] Identify owner funding, reimbursements, withdrawals and inter-account transfers without assuming their classification.
  • [ ] Check bank charges, reversals, duplicate-looking lines and transactions dated near period-end.
  • [ ] List every unresolved item with amount, date, reference, evidence checked, owner and next action.
  • [ ] Carry forward open items and check whether later statements or documents resolve them.
  • [ ] Save the reconciliation schedule with the statement and linked supporting evidence.
  • [ ] Review exceptions with the responsible manager, bookkeeper or qualified adviser as appropriate.

The schedule should make it possible for another reviewer to understand what was matched, what remains open and why. Keep notes factual: “invoice requested from manager” is more useful than “probably maintenance.” If an item affects earlier periods or appears repeatedly, flag it for a broader review instead of clearing it with an unsupported adjustment.

When a cleanup or adviser review may help

Repeated unmatched transactions, missing prior-period statements, account activity mixed with personal spending, or opening figures that cannot be supported may call for a scoped bookkeeping cleanup. The work can include gathering records, tracing cash movements, preparing an open-item schedule and documenting what remains unverified. The scope and planning period should adapt to the number of accounts, transaction history, available evidence and response time of people supplying documents; no fixed turnaround should be assumed.

Bali Accounting’s villa bookkeeping cleanup service is a relevant commercial option when older villa records need investigation and organization. Bookkeeping preparation is separate from tax advice or submission work. Any tax treatment or filing question should go to a qualified, appropriately authorised adviser under a separate engagement. To discuss an appropriate scope, contact the Client Advisory team through Get Started.

General information only: This article offers general bookkeeping information, not tax, legal or individualized professional advice. It is not a substitute for reviewing your records or speaking with a qualified adviser. No tax treatment is determined by the illustrative example.

Frequently asked questions

What should I do first when a bank transaction does not match?

Check the account, period, amount, date and reference, then search the relevant statement, invoice, payout report or transfer confirmation. Log what you checked and what is missing. Do not change an amount just to force a match.

Is an unmatched transaction always an error?

No. It may be a timing difference, bank charge, refund, currency-related difference or incomplete record. Treat it as unresolved until evidence supports an explanation, and keep any open item visible for follow-up.

Can an OTA payout be matched directly to one booking?

Sometimes, but a settlement can combine reservations and reflect fees, refunds or other adjustments. Compare the payout statement with reservation-level evidence and the bank receipt rather than assuming the deposited amount equals one booking’s gross value.

How often should a villa bank account be reconciled?

Choose a cadence that fits the business’s reporting and review process, transaction activity and evidence availability. A regular close helps keep differences manageable, but this article does not set a mandatory deadline.

Does bank reconciliation determine the tax treatment of a transaction?

No. Reconciliation helps establish and document cash movements; it does not decide tax treatment. Prepare the relevant evidence and questions for a qualified Indonesian tax adviser.
