title: Villa Payroll Records: Staff Advances and Expense Reimbursements
primaryKeyword: villa payroll bookkeeping staff advances reimbursements
contentHtml:
Villa payroll bookkeeping staff advances reimbursements work best when each payment has a clear purpose, named recipient, approval trail and settlement record. Keep a staff advance distinct from salary and from a reimbursement for an expense the employee has already paid. Record what happened, match it to the bank or cash movement, and refer uncertain treatment to the responsible payroll or tax adviser.

Who this applies to

This guide is for Bali villa owners, operators and bookkeepers who handle staff-related cash outside the regular wage payment: for example, a housekeeping or maintenance employee receives money to buy supplies, or pays for an approved business purchase and later asks to be repaid. It is also useful where a manager pays staff from a petty-cash float or company card and sends receipts to the finance desk afterward.

The goal here is reliable bookkeeping evidence, not a decision about Indonesian employment, payroll, tax or social-security treatment. How a payment should be classified may depend on the facts, the working arrangement, company policy and current requirements. Where the distinction could affect payroll reporting or an employee’s entitlements, ask the suitably qualified, authorised adviser before deciding how to process it.

These controls are especially useful when several villas share staff, staff make purchases at different properties, receipts arrive in more than one language, or the person approving spending is not the person entering the books. If an owner or manager pays a staff cost personally, record that funding separately rather than disguising it as a staff reimbursement. The evidence should show both who paid and which entity or property benefited.

Separate advances, reimbursements and payroll records

A staff advance is money provided before the employee has completed the purchase or accounted for the funds. The record should show the amount issued, reason, recipient, date, approving person, expected supporting evidence and how any unused amount is to be returned or otherwise resolved. Until the employee accounts for it, show it on an open-item schedule rather than silently treating it as a final expense.

A reimbursement is generally a repayment for an expense already paid by an employee on the business’s behalf. Its support should connect the employee’s claim to the supplier receipt, the business purpose, the property or department, approval and the actual reimbursement transfer. A receipt alone may not tell you who initially paid, whether the purchase was for the villa, or if it has already been claimed. Keep those details with the document.

Payroll records are a separate evidence stream. Keep the approved payroll summary and payment evidence together, while retaining a separate register for advances and reimbursements. If an item might be a wage adjustment, deduction, allowance or other payroll component, don’t decide its treatment merely because it appears in a staff payment list. Flag it for the responsible payroll or tax adviser, and retain the written instruction that informs the final processing.

A practical register can use one row per movement, with a unique reference such as “ADV-2026-014” or “REIMB-2026-021.” Record the employee identifier, not unnecessary personal information; date; amount; currency; purpose; property or cost centre; payment method; approver; evidence location; status; and any settlement date. Keep the underlying documents in a controlled folder with access limited to people who need them.

For related controls around invoices, payroll schedules and supporting records, see the Bali villa payroll and supplier invoice control workflow. For a recurring operating rhythm, the control calendar for Bali villa accounts can help owners assign collection and review tasks. The service scope for villa payroll records should be confirmed separately, including whether any processing or submission work is included.

Build an evidence trail that can be followed

Evidence should let a reviewer follow the transaction from request to final settlement without relying on someone’s memory. For an advance, retain the request or task note, approval, cash or bank transfer proof, receipts for purchases, a short reconciliation and evidence of any balance returned. For a reimbursement, keep the claim, receipt or supplier invoice, proof the employee paid, approval and the repayment transfer. Use one reference consistently across the register, receipt files and bank description where practical.

Receipts can be faded, small, or issued as a paper slip. Capture a legible copy promptly and preserve the original according to the business’s record policy. If a document is missing, note that fact and request a replacement or other evidence. Do not fabricate a receipt, alter a source document or mark an item “complete” merely because the cash was paid. An exception log should state what is missing, who is following up and whether the item remains unresolved.

For shared staff or multi-property operations, record the villa or cost centre benefiting from each purchase. If one trip covers supplies for two properties, retain the detail supporting the split and the allocation method used. Don’t divide a total by guesswork and imply that the allocation came from the receipt. Where supporting detail is inadequate, keep it visible as an open question for the manager rather than presenting an unsupported allocation as settled fact.

Match each payment to the bank statement or petty-cash record, then check that the transaction date, amount, payee and reference agree. If a bank transfer settles a batch of claims, preserve the batch breakdown so each staff item can be traced to the single cash movement. If cash is used, a signed acknowledgement or equivalent record should establish who received it, how much, and when. Restrict cash handling and review responsibilities where the team’s size makes separation practical.

Good record keeping also protects employee privacy. Payroll and claim folders should not be broadly shared with villa operations staff. Use a consistent staff identifier in working schedules where names are not necessary, keep sensitive personal details in the appropriate restricted location, and follow the company’s retention and access policies. Avoid sending unprotected payroll files through informal group chats if a controlled method is available.

Illustrative IDR example: reconcile, don’t guess

The following example is illustrative only and shows cash movement arithmetic, not a payroll or tax calculation. A villa business gives a staff member an advance of IDR 500,000 for approved cleaning supplies. The employee submits supplier receipts totalling IDR 320,000 and returns the unused IDR 180,000 to the business cash box. Separately, the employee submits an approved IDR 75,000 transport reimbursement for a documented business errand that they paid personally.

Illustrative cash movements and evidence status
MovementCash amountEvidence to match
Advance paid to employeeIDR 500,000 outApproved request and transfer or signed cash acknowledgement
Supplies bought with advanceIDR 320,000 accounted forSupplier receipts and business purpose
Unused advance returnedIDR 180,000 inCash receipt or bank deposit evidence
Separate approved transport reimbursementIDR 75,000 outClaim, receipt or journey evidence, approval and payment proof

The advance clears arithmetically because IDR 320,000 of supported purchases plus IDR 180,000 returned equals IDR 500,000 issued. Across these described movements, total cash paid out is IDR 575,000: the IDR 500,000 advance plus the separate IDR 75,000 reimbursement. The IDR 180,000 return reduces the net cash outflow to IDR 395,000, which also equals the IDR 320,000 supplies plus IDR 75,000 transport. This is a selected evidence schedule, not a trial balance, full payroll record or instruction to post a journal entry.

In the register, show the advance as settled only once the purchase evidence and returned balance are reviewed and matched. Keep the transport claim on its own line because it has a different purpose and evidence trail. If the IDR 180,000 return is not found, do not claim that the advance is fully reconciled; record the unreconciled amount, ask the responsible manager to investigate and retain the resolution evidence when obtained.

Monthly review and handover

At each agreed close, compare the register with bank statements, cash counts, payroll summaries and available supporting documents. Review both completed items and open balances. A useful summary distinguishes new advances, reimbursements paid, amounts returned, claims awaiting approval, missing documentation and old items that need a decision. The review should explain what remains outstanding, not bury it in a general expense total.

Set a practical internal rhythm suited to the operation. For example, a villa might collect receipts during the week, have a manager approve claims before a regular bookkeeping close, and review unresolved advances at month-end. This is a planning example, not a guaranteed turnaround time or a statutory deadline. Agree who is responsible, when staff should submit documents under company policy, and how urgent purchases are handled without bypassing later review.

A clean handover includes the register, evidence index, approvals, payment records, unresolved-item log and a concise note explaining unusual movements. The note might state that a receipt is pending, a refund has not yet reached the bank, or the villa allocation needs manager confirmation. Keep the original evidence accessible rather than sending only a spreadsheet with unexplained totals.

When preparing for a bookkeeper or adviser, distinguish bookkeeping support from payroll administration, tax compliance or submission activity. Those tasks may require a separate engagement and action by the responsible authorised person; monthly bookkeeping does not automatically include them. For a broader close process, use the villa month-end record-collection workflow as a companion reference. Bali Accounting’s Client Advisory team can discuss an agreed scope through the get-started page.

What owners get wrong

  • Correction 1: “Every staff payment is payroll.” A payment’s label in a bank feed does not establish what it represents. Separate advance, reimbursement and payroll evidence; refer ambiguous items to the qualified adviser responsible for classification.
  • Correction 2: “A receipt proves the business owes the employee.” A receipt supports a purchase but may not prove the employee paid, the villa benefited, the expense was approved, or repayment occurred. Add the claim, purpose, approval and proof of payment.
  • Correction 3: “An advance is cleared when receipts arrive.” Receipts account only for the documented portion. Compare total supported spending with the amount issued and record returned funds or the remaining open balance. Keep follow-up visible until evidence supports resolution.

A further control failure is using a payroll spreadsheet as the only record for staff cash. That can blur wage calculations with petty cash, conceal outstanding advances and make a payment impossible to trace. Keep a distinct schedule linked to payroll where appropriate, and preserve both records so an authorised reviewer can see how they relate without assuming they are the same transaction.

Printable staff advance and reimbursement checklist

Use this as an adaptable desk checklist. Tailor approval levels, submission practices and storage to the business’s internal policy and adviser instructions. Check each line for the particular transaction; do not treat a completed checklist as a substitute for missing evidence.

  1. Identify the payment: assign a reference, name or staff identifier, date, currency and amount; mark whether it is an advance, reimbursement, cash float movement or an item awaiting classification.
  2. Record the business purpose: note the errand, purchase or villa task and the property or cost centre benefiting. Ask for clarification if the description is too vague to assess.
  3. Confirm approval: retain the request and the appropriate manager’s approval. Record any exception to the normal approval path and who authorised it.
  4. Match cash movement: attach the bank transfer, cash acknowledgement, cash-box record or returned-funds evidence. Check the amount and date against the relevant statement or count.
  5. Collect supporting documents: keep supplier receipts, invoices, claim details and evidence of employee payment where relevant. Log missing or unclear documents instead of filling gaps with assumptions.
  6. Reconcile an advance: compare the amount issued with supported spending and returned funds. Record any difference as open, with an owner and follow-up note.
  7. Review reimbursements separately: check the business purpose, supporting evidence, approval and repayment proof. Check that the same claim has not been recorded twice.
  8. Keep payroll distinct: link relevant schedules if useful, but do not decide wage or tax treatment from bookkeeping labels. Escalate uncertain items to the authorised payroll or tax adviser.
  9. Protect and file: store evidence under the transaction reference in an access-controlled location, using the company’s document and privacy policies.
  10. Close with open items: reconcile to bank and cash records, list what remains unresolved, and include that list in the monthly handover or management review.

General information only; this article is not tax, payroll, employment or legal advice, and it is not individual advice or evidence of professional review. Requirements and treatment depend on the facts and may change. Consult a suitably qualified, authorised Indonesian adviser about your circumstances. Any preparation or submission work requires the responsible authorised person and a separate engagement; it is not automatically included in monthly bookkeeping.

Frequently asked questions

Should a staff advance be recorded as an expense immediately?

Keep the advance identifiable and open until its use and any returned balance are supported. The correct accounting treatment depends on the facts and the entity’s policies, so have the responsible bookkeeper or adviser confirm classification.

What documents support a staff reimbursement?

Keep the employee’s claim, supplier receipt or other evidence, business purpose, property or cost centre, approval and proof of repayment. A receipt by itself may not show who paid or whether the purchase served the villa.

How should an unused advance be handled?

Document the return with cash-box, acknowledgement or bank evidence and match it to the original advance reference. If it has not been returned or otherwise accounted for, leave it visible as an open item and follow up.

Can reimbursements be included in a payroll file?

You may link the schedules for review, but keep the supporting records distinct. If a payment could be a payroll component or affect payroll reporting, ask the responsible qualified adviser rather than deciding from its label.

Does bookkeeping automatically include payroll processing or filings?

No. Confirm the scope in writing. Payroll administration, tax compliance and any submission work are separately scoped and require action by the responsible authorised person; they are not an automatic inclusion in monthly bookkeeping.

How often should a villa review advances and claims?

Choose an internal review rhythm that fits transaction volume, staffing and the agreed close process. A regular review helps surface missing evidence and old balances, but any schedule here is a planning choice, not a guaranteed turnaround or mandatory deadline.

title: PT PMA Setup in Bali: Record the First Business Transactions
primaryKeyword: pt pma setup bali first business transactions
contentHtml:
For a new PT PMA in Bali, record each first transaction from the bank evidence outward: identify who paid, which legal entity benefited, what the payment was for, and whether it is company income, a company cost, owner funding, a refundable amount or another balance-sheet item. Keep the invoice, agreement, bank statement and approval together. Do not treat a payment into the company bank account as revenue merely because cash arrived.

This approach gives the company a usable starting record without guessing tax treatment or creating unsupported accounting entries. It also makes later bookkeeping, management reporting and discussion with an authorised Indonesian adviser more efficient.

Who this applies to

This guide is for founders, directors, remote owners and operating teams involved in a new or recently activated PT PMA, particularly where the company will operate or manage a Bali villa, hospitality activity or property-related service. It is useful whether the first payment is made by an owner, a local supplier, a guest, a platform or another group company.

It also applies when formation work is complete enough for the company to begin receiving funds but the operational systems are still being organised. Company formation, licensing, tax registration, tax-compliance work and bookkeeping are related but distinct scopes. A formation provider may help establish the entity, while the responsible authorised person must confirm regulatory and tax questions separately.

If the company has already had payments before its bookkeeping system was opened, create an evidence-led opening period rather than backdating assumptions. A flexible onboarding plan might begin with the date the company bank account became usable, then extend earlier if formation costs, owner advances or pre-opening commitments need to be documented. The period and sequence should be agreed for the actual records available; they are planning choices, not guaranteed turnaround times.

What to collect before recording anything

Start with a transaction register and an evidence index. Give every item a reference, date, amount, currency, bank account, payer or recipient, business purpose and current classification. Mark uncertain items as questions instead of forcing them into an income or expense category.

  • Entity evidence: company name, bank-account details, formation documents, shareholder or director approvals and relevant contracts.
  • Bank evidence: complete statements, transfer confirmations, payment references and details of any account used before the company account opened.
  • Supplier evidence: invoices, receipts, purchase orders, contracts, delivery records and proof of payment.
  • Owner-funding evidence: the contributor, date, amount, purpose, currency and written basis for capital, loan, reimbursement or another funding arrangement.
  • Revenue evidence: guest invoices, booking reports, platform statements, management agreements, cancellation records and payout confirmations.
  • Property evidence: lease or management agreements, asset purchase documents, renovation approvals, handover records and records showing whether a cost belongs to the company or another party.

Use consistent file names, such as date, counterparty, amount and evidence type. Preserve the original Indonesian document where applicable and add an explanatory note only when needed. A translated summary can help management, but it does not replace the source record.

How to classify the first transactions

The first question is not “which expense account should I use?” It is “what economic event occurred?” A company may receive money without earning revenue, and it may incur a business cost without paying it immediately. Those distinctions matter when a PT PMA is funded by its owners or when pre-opening suppliers accept deposits.

Illustrative first-transaction review table
TransactionEvidence to retainQuestion before classification
Owner transfers money to the companyBank record, funding note, approval and agreement if applicableIs this capital, a loan, reimbursement funding or another owner balance?
Company pays a supplier depositInvoice or quotation, contract, payment proof and delivery termsIs the amount refundable, an advance for future services or a cost already received?
Company receives a guest or platform payoutReservation report, platform statement, fee detail and bank receiptWhat is the underlying booking activity, and which deductions or liabilities remain?
Director pays a company bill personallySupplier invoice, proof of personal payment and reimbursement approvalIs the company recognising a payable to the director rather than recording company cash?
Company buys equipmentInvoice, delivery evidence, serial number and payment recordIs this an operating supply, an asset or property-related spending requiring adviser review?

Do not solve uncertainty by using “miscellaneous expense” for everything. A temporary review category and a missing-document register are safer than a confident but unsupported classification. Once the evidence is obtained, update the classification with a note explaining what changed.

An illustrative IDR cash-movement example

The following is a deliberately limited cash schedule, not a trial balance and not a set of balancing journal entries. It demonstrates how to describe movements without claiming that every amount is income or expense.

Assume a new PT PMA’s company bank account shows these illustrative movements during its first operating period:

  • Owner transfer into the company bank account: IDR 150,000,000.
  • Office and formation-related supplier payment from the company account: IDR 12,000,000.
  • Refundable venue or service deposit paid from the company account: IDR 20,000,000.
  • Guest-related payout received after platform deductions: IDR 38,000,000.
  • Utilities and operating supplies paid from the company account: IDR 8,000,000.

The arithmetic of the bank movement is: IDR 150,000,000 minus IDR 12,000,000 minus IDR 20,000,000 plus IDR 38,000,000 minus IDR 8,000,000 equals IDR 148,000,000 closing cash, assuming no other movements and no opening cash.

That closing cash does not mean the company earned IDR 148,000,000. The owner transfer may be funding rather than revenue; the refundable deposit may remain an asset or recoverable amount; the guest payout may need to be reconciled to gross booking evidence and platform deductions; and the supplier payments require their own classification. The schedule proves only the stated cash movements. The supporting documents determine how those movements are presented in the accounting records.

For a useful review file, attach the five bank lines to an evidence schedule with columns for reference, counterparty, purpose, proposed classification, evidence received, unresolved question and reviewer decision. If the owner transfer was made partly for a supplier payment and partly as working capital, document those facts rather than treating the entire transfer as one unexplained amount.

Recording owner funding and personal payments

Owner funding is one of the most important early distinctions. A transfer from a shareholder does not automatically represent paid-in capital, and an amount paid by a director personally does not disappear simply because the company received the benefit. The written arrangement, approvals, bank trail and local professional advice should determine the appropriate treatment.

Create a funding register with the contributor, date, amount, currency, destination, stated purpose, supporting agreement and status. Separate amounts intended for company working capital from amounts that are reimbursements, advances or payments on behalf of the company. Where a founder pays a supplier personally, retain both the supplier invoice and evidence that the founder paid it. Record the company’s obligation or reimbursement status according to the agreed treatment.

Do not net owner funding against company costs in a spreadsheet. That shortcut hides the source of cash and makes it difficult to explain what the company owes, owns or has received. A clear register can be handed to the bookkeeper and, where needed, to a licensed adviser for review.

What owners get wrong

  1. Calling every incoming transfer revenue. Correction: trace the payer and purpose. Owner funding, security deposits, intercompany amounts and guest receipts can have different accounting consequences. Keep the evidence and flag the classification question.
  2. Recording only the amount that reached the bank. Correction: reconcile platform or payment-provider statements to the underlying booking, fees, refunds and reserves. A net payout is a cash fact, not automatically the full description of the transaction.
  3. Using the owner’s personal account as an invisible company account. Correction: list each pre-account payment separately, identify the person who paid, preserve the invoice and decide whether the company owes that person or whether another arrangement applies. Move future company activity through the company account where practical.

Another frequent mistake is opening the books with an unexplained “starting balance.” If a balance predates the bookkeeping period, prepare an evidence schedule showing how it was established. Do not invent journal entries merely to make totals appear neat.

A practical first-period workflow

Use an adaptable workflow rather than waiting for every process to be perfect.

  1. Define the cut-off: agree the first period to review and list activity before that date that may affect the opening position.
  2. Secure access: obtain read-only or appropriately controlled access to company bank accounts, booking platforms, payment providers and shared document folders.
  3. Export original records: download statements and reports for the full period, retaining dates and report names.
  4. Build the register: list every bank line and known non-bank commitment, including unpaid invoices and deposits.
  5. Match evidence: connect each line to an invoice, contract, statement, approval or explanatory note.
  6. Separate questions: distinguish missing evidence, bookkeeping classification issues and matters for a licensed tax or legal adviser.
  7. Review exceptions: investigate duplicates, personal payments, unexplained transfers, foreign-currency differences and amounts that do not match supplier or platform records.
  8. Approve the close: retain a short list of unresolved items, responsible person and next action. Do not silently overwrite the history when new evidence arrives.

For owners who need structured support, Bali Accounting’s PT PMA company formation service can be considered alongside a separately scoped bookkeeping engagement. A Client Advisory conversation through Get started can help clarify which records and services belong in each scope.

Printable first-transactions checklist

Print or copy this list into the company’s opening-period file.

  • Entity: confirm the legal company name, account holder and operating purpose.
  • Bank: obtain complete statements, transfer confirmations and opening or pre-opening activity.
  • Owners: list every contribution, personal payment and reimbursement request.
  • Suppliers: collect invoices, contracts, deposits, delivery evidence and unpaid bills.
  • Revenue: collect booking reports, guest invoices, platform statements, refunds and payout confirmations.
  • Property: identify which costs relate to the company, owner, landlord, manager or another entity.
  • Classification: mark each item as proposed company income, cost, asset, liability, owner funding or unresolved.
  • Reconciliation: compare the transaction register with the bank statement and investigate every difference.
  • Evidence: assign a file reference and record what is missing.
  • Adviser questions: prepare specific questions about ownership, contracts, funding, tax treatment, licensing or regulatory obligations.
  • Approval: record who reviewed the opening schedule and which items remain open.

For related guidance, see PT PMA owner funding records in Bali, the PT PMA villa records handover checklist and the Bali villa month-end close workflow. These articles address record preparation and controls, not individual tax or legal conclusions.

General information disclaimer: This article is general bookkeeping information for planning and record organisation. It is not tax, legal, accounting, licensing, immigration or investment advice, and it is not evidence of professional review. Tax and regulatory treatment depends on the facts and should be confirmed with the responsible authorised person or licensed Indonesian adviser. Preparation or submission work requires a separate engagement and is not automatically included in monthly bookkeeping.

Frequently asked questions

Should the first owner transfer be recorded as revenue?

No. Identify its purpose and supporting arrangement first. It may be capital, a loan, an advance, reimbursement funding or another owner-related balance. The correct treatment requires evidence and, where relevant, authorised professional advice.

What if the company paid a supplier before its bank account was ready?

List the payment separately, retain the supplier evidence and identify who actually paid. The records should show the company benefit and the resulting amount owed or other agreed treatment rather than hiding the payment in an unexplained opening balance.

Is a platform payout the same as booking revenue?

Not necessarily. A payout is a cash receipt after whatever deductions, refunds or reserves the platform applied. Reconcile it to the reservation and platform statements before deciding how the underlying activity should be recorded.

Can a spreadsheet be enough for a new PT PMA?

A spreadsheet can be a useful evidence register during onboarding, but it should not replace complete source documents, bank reconciliation, a controlled accounting process and appropriate review. The required system depends on transaction volume and reporting needs.

When should a tax adviser review the first transactions?

Ask for review when funding structure, property rights, cross-border payments, contracts, withholding questions or regulatory classification could affect the company. Bookkeeping can organise the facts, but an authorised adviser must assess the applicable position.

title: Bookkeeper vs Tax Consultant in Bali: Who Does What?
primaryKeyword: bookkeeper vs tax consultant bali responsibilities
contentHtml:
A bookkeeper maintains organised, reconciled financial records; a tax consultant interprets those records against the applicable tax position and advises on compliance or planning. For a Bali villa, the safest arrangement is usually coordinated work: the bookkeeper builds an evidence-based record of bookings, payouts, expenses, owner funding and cash, while the authorised tax professional assesses treatment and handles separately agreed tax work. Neither role should be assumed to replace the other.

Who this applies to

This distinction matters to foreign owners, Indonesian owners, PT PMA operators, villa management companies and anyone receiving income through online travel agencies, direct bookings or a local manager. It is especially useful when one person informally performs several jobs. A property manager may send payout statements, an internal administrator may enter invoices, and a tax consultant may request schedules. Those contributions are valuable, but they do not automatically mean the books have been independently reconciled or that tax advice has been provided.

It also applies when an owner is changing providers, starting a new reporting period or preparing records for a licensed adviser. Begin by identifying the legal entity, bank accounts, booking channels, property arrangements and people responsible for approvals. Then agree which work is recurring bookkeeping, which work is advisory, and which work requires a separate engagement with the responsible authorised person.

Bali Accounting’s tax compliance service should be understood in that scoped context. Preparation and submission work are not automatic inclusions in monthly bookkeeping. Ask for the exact deliverables, responsible person, review process and source records before work begins.

What a bookkeeper handles

Bookkeeping is the disciplined process of turning source documents and cash activity into a consistent financial record. The work is operational and evidence-led. Depending on the engagement, a bookkeeper may:

  • collect bank statements, payment processor reports, invoices, receipts and booking records;
  • enter transactions using an agreed chart of accounts;
  • reconcile bank movements to the accounting record;
  • match OTA reservation activity, commissions, refunds, reserves and payouts;
  • separate company revenue from money held for owners, guests or suppliers;
  • record and track owner contributions, advances, reimbursements and withdrawals;
  • identify missing documents, unexplained differences and duplicate entries;
  • prepare monthly management reports, open-item schedules and supporting evidence indexes.

A competent bookkeeper does not simply copy the amount that arrived in a bank account into a revenue line. A payout may be net of commission, a guest deposit may be refundable, and an owner transfer may not be income. The record should show what the movement represents and point back to evidence.

For practical context, compare this with what a Bali villa bookkeeper does each month. A monthly close is useful only when the underlying bank, booking and supplier records are available and exceptions are documented rather than silently estimated.

What a tax consultant handles

A tax consultant examines the facts, entity structure, transactions and available evidence to advise on tax classification, obligations, calculations, compliance decisions or planning within the consultant’s authorised scope. The consultant may:

  • ask how the business, property, owner and manager are legally connected;
  • assess whether particular receipts, costs or payments require a specific tax treatment;
  • review relevant registration, reporting and payment questions;
  • identify information needed for a tax return, statement or other submission;
  • explain assumptions, unresolved facts and records that could change the advice;
  • prepare or review tax work where that task is expressly included in a separate engagement;
  • communicate with the responsible authority when properly authorised to do so.

Tax advice is not created merely by placing a tax label beside a bookkeeping entry. A bookkeeper can flag a payment as an issue for adviser review, but should not infer a tax conclusion from the label alone. Likewise, a tax consultant can explain the required treatment but may not be responsible for entering, reconciling or maintaining every underlying transaction.

Questions about withholding, rental income, residency, related parties, cross-border payments, entity status or deductions should be put to a qualified Indonesian tax adviser who has the full facts. Avoid relying on a general article, an old spreadsheet or an informal verbal assumption as the final position.

Where the responsibilities connect

The handover between the two roles is where many villa records weaken. A tax consultant needs more than a bank balance. A bookkeeper needs clear instructions when a tax professional determines that an item must be presented or separated in a particular way. The connection should therefore be documented.

Illustrative division of work for a Bali villa
Work areaBookkeeper’s roleTax consultant’s role
Booking incomeReconcile reservation reports, fees, refunds and depositsAssess relevant tax classification and reporting implications
Supplier costsCollect invoices, code costs and track unpaid itemsAdvise on treatment where facts or rules require assessment
Owner fundingMaintain a schedule distinguishing advances, capital, loans and reimbursementsConsider entity, documentation and tax consequences
Bank accountsReconcile statements and investigate unexplained movementsUse reliable records when reviewing compliance questions
Tax submissionSupply agreed schedules and evidence, if includedPrepare, review or submit only under a separate agreed scope

The owner remains responsible for providing accurate information and approving decisions. A useful handover pack may include a transaction listing, bank reconciliations, booking-to-payout schedules, supplier register, owner-funding schedule, fixed-asset evidence, missing-document register and a list of questions requiring adviser judgment.

For a deeper preparation framework, see preparing records for a Bali tax consultant. If the provider is changing, also review the bookkeeping handover process so opening information is explained rather than merely exported.

Illustrative IDR worked example: follow the cash, not just the payout

The following is an illustrative evidence schedule, not a tax calculation and not a complete set of accounts. Assume a villa’s booking report for one selected period shows guest charges of IDR 24,000,000. An OTA deducts an IDR 2,400,000 commission and sends IDR 21,600,000 to the business bank account. The business then pays IDR 5,000,000 to a cleaner and supplier, and transfers IDR 4,000,000 to the owner as a documented withdrawal.

Selected illustrative cash movements
MovementAmountEvidence to retain
Guest charges shown on booking reportIDR 24,000,000Reservation or platform report
OTA commission deductedIDR 2,400,000Commission statement or invoice
Bank payout receivedIDR 21,600,000Bank statement and payout report
Supplier paymentIDR 5,000,000Invoice, approval and bank movement
Owner withdrawalIDR 4,000,000Transfer record and owner schedule

The arithmetic is: IDR 24,000,000 minus IDR 2,400,000 equals IDR 21,600,000 received. After the selected supplier payment and owner withdrawal, the bank movement left from this small example is IDR 12,600,000, because IDR 21,600,000 minus IDR 5,000,000 minus IDR 4,000,000 equals IDR 12,600,000. That figure is not profit, taxable income or a closing bank balance. It excludes other activity and simply demonstrates why a bookkeeper preserves the gross booking evidence, deducted fee, supplier payment and owner movement separately. A tax consultant then considers the relevant facts and treatment.

What owners get wrong

1. Treating the bank receipt as the whole income record

Correction: retain the gross reservation evidence, deductions, refunds, timing differences and payout confirmation. Ask the bookkeeper to reconcile the components. Ask the tax consultant how the resulting classification should be considered, rather than assuming the net deposit answers every question.

2. Expecting a bookkeeper to give definitive tax advice

Correction: maintain a questions list for the authorised tax adviser. The bookkeeper can describe the transaction and its supporting documents; the adviser decides what requires tax analysis within the engagement.

3. Assuming a tax consultant maintains complete operational books

Correction: confirm whether transaction entry, bank reconciliation, invoice collection, management reporting and owner schedules are included. Tax review based on incomplete records can leave avoidable gaps, so agree who owns each recurring control.

A practical onboarding and monthly workflow

An onboarding period should be an adaptable planning example, not a guaranteed turnaround time. A sensible sequence may be adjusted for the number of villas, missing records, entity structure, bank access and the tax consultant’s review timetable.

  1. Define scope. List entities, properties, accounts, booking channels, reporting periods and deliverables. Separate recurring bookkeeping from advisory and submission work.
  2. Collect evidence. Gather bank statements, platform reports, invoices, contracts, owner transfers, payroll-related records where relevant, and prior reports. Do not treat an unsupported spreadsheet as final evidence.
  3. Map responsibility. Assign transaction entry, approval, reconciliation, document follow-up, tax questions and submission authority to named roles or teams.
  4. Resolve opening issues. Prepare a missing-document register and explanation of inherited balances. Do not create balancing entries merely to make a report appear complete.
  5. Run a sample close. Test selected bank movements, one or more payout reconciliations, supplier evidence and owner transactions. Record exceptions and agree how they will be handled.
  6. Prepare the adviser pack. Give the tax consultant reconciled schedules, source documents, entity information and a concise list of judgment questions.
  7. Document decisions. Keep written notes of assumptions, adviser conclusions, unresolved items and the period to which each decision applies.

Frequently asked questions

Can one provider be both the bookkeeper and tax consultant?

Sometimes a firm offers both functions, but the scope and responsible person should still be clear. Ask whether bookkeeping, review, advice, preparation and submission are separate deliverables, and confirm what evidence and approvals each requires.

Should a tax consultant receive the full bank statements?

Usually the adviser needs sufficient evidence to understand the relevant transactions, but the exact pack depends on the engagement and facts. A reconciled bank schedule with source statements, explanations and open items is more useful than isolated screenshots.

Is a villa manager a substitute for a bookkeeper?

Not automatically. A manager may provide operational records, approve costs or administer payouts, while a bookkeeper performs independent classification and reconciliation. Agree controls so the person making payments is not the only person explaining them.

What should an owner do when records are incomplete?

Start a missing-document register, preserve available bank and platform evidence, identify assumptions and avoid presenting estimates as confirmed records. Then ask the bookkeeper and tax consultant which gaps matter most for their respective work.

Does monthly bookkeeping include tax filing?

Not necessarily. Filing, tax calculations, advice and communications with an authority should be expressly included in a separate agreed scope where applicable. Confirm the responsible authorised person and required approvals before relying on any submission arrangement.
